questions.question: When does the catch block run in Java?
options: Always, before the try block
When an exception is thrown inside the try block
Only when the program finishes without errors
After the finally block no matter what happens
explanations: The catch block does not run before try; it runs afterward when there is an exception.
Correct. The catch block runs only when an exception matching the type declared in the catch is thrown.
If the program finishes without errors, the catch block does not run.
The finally block runs after catch, not the other way around.

questions.question: What does the finally block do?
options: It runs only if an exception occurs in the try block
It always runs, whether an exception occurs or not
It runs only when no catch block is defined
It runs only the first time the method is called
explanations: The finally block is not limited to when an exception occurs; it always runs.
Correct. The finally block always runs after the try-catch, regardless of whether an exception was thrown or not.
The finally block always runs, not just when there is no catch block.
The finally block runs on every pass through the try-catch, not just the first time.

questions.question: Can you have multiple catch blocks in Java?
options: No, you can only have one catch block per try
Yes, but they must go from most specific to most general
Only if you use the multi-catch keyword
Only when using unchecked exceptions
explanations: It is possible to have multiple catch blocks; the idea of having only one is incorrect.
Correct. You can have multiple catch blocks, and they must be ordered from most specific (e.g. FileNotFoundException) to most general (e.g. IOException).
Multi-catch lets you combine types, but it is not the only way to handle multiple exceptions.
The ordering of multiple catch blocks does not depend on whether the exceptions are checked or unchecked.

questions.question: What does multi-catch syntax do in Java?
options: It allows a single catch block to handle multiple exception types with the syntax catch(A | B e)
It allows throwing multiple exceptions at once
It allows having multiple finally blocks in a single try
It allows a method to return multiple error types
explanations: Correct. Multi-catch lets you handle multiple exception types in a single catch block using the | operator, for example: catch(IOException | SQLException e).
Multi-catch does not throw exceptions; it catches them.
You can only have one finally block per try.
Multi-catch does not affect the method's return value.

questions.question: What is try-with-resources in Java?
options: A try block that uses less memory than a normal try
A way to declare resources that close automatically when leaving the block
A pattern to reuse the same resource across multiple methods
An alternative to using constructors to create objects
explanations: Try-with-resources has nothing to do with memory usage.
Correct. try-with-resources (try(Resource r = ...) { }) declares a resource that closes automatically when the block ends, without the need to call close() manually.
Try-with-resources closes the resource when leaving, it does not reuse it between methods.
Try-with-resources is used for resources (streams, connections), not to replace constructors.
